content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of optimizing the microarchitecture of a RISC-V processor, in terms of power consumption, performance and area. Computing these metrics require a large amount of time, so the paper first presents a method to approximate them, based on known approximation models. The predictions of these models are used as features for an XGBoost model, which is trained on real RISC-V data to obtain a better prediction. Next the optimization metric is defined as a weighted sum of the three metrics (power, performance and area), and an RL actor-critic method is used to find an optimal solution. This is done for 6 types of RISC-V architectures (not all of them with the same optimization weights). The rsults show significant improvements in performance/power or performance/area compared with 5 previous methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper considers an interesting problem and provides interesting results. However, it has several weaknesses that should be addressed.
- The general idea of the paper is similar to the paper of Mirhoseini et al (Nature, 2021). That paper should be cited and discussed.
- The approximation models are evaluated using MAPE and Kendal's Tau. What are the RMSE and Pearson correlation?
- It is unclear whether the final results were evaluated using the approximation models or an actual EDA run. If the former is the case, actual EDA runs should be done to measure the actual quality of the results.
- Different weight vectors were used for different architectures. What would have happened if equal weights were used for all of them? (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). There should be some sensitivity analysis to make sure the results do not hold for specific selections of weights.
- The run-times of the various methods were not the same, some ran less time than the proposed method. What would happen if the new method is only allowed to run for the duration of the second-best method in each case? Would it still outperform it?
- What is the size of the optimization space considered for each architecture? How does it relate to the sizes of more complex architectures mentioned, such as x86 or ARM?
- The approximation models used for the objectives are from over a decade ago, it would be good to provide a reference stating that they are still the state of the art.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper applies a similar idea to the idea of Mirhoseini et al to a different but related problem. The code is not provided, so the results are not fully reproducible. The paper is mostly clear. Regarding the quality, I have the above concerns.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper applies a recently developed idea to an important problem. However, the quality and significance of the results are unclear, due to the concerns raised above. I will reconsider my recommendation based on the authors response to the issues raised above and based on providing additional experimental results (other weight vectors, equal run-time, evaluation by EDA).
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for combining reinforcement learning and using it to search out potential microarchitecture designs for performance improvements in processor designs. The motivation here is to be able to use RL inside of a realistic enough simulation environment to explore possible micro protector designs faster than using human experts to design these types of components. The paper focuses on a particular part of the CPU structure related to the microarchitecture and design to perform several experiments and evaluate the performance compared to area and power consumption of such designs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
pros
- This work does create a complex simulation and design exploration system that is combined with an RL algorithm to search potential architecture designs.
- The method does produce some designs that appear to have improved performance.

Cons
- The novelty of the work is unclear. There is prior work on computational architecture design. Also, many sections of the paper lack enough detail to understand how it compares to prior work.
- More detail on why the RL algorithm was chosen for this problem and how the simulation and network were chosen are required to fully understand the method and allow the community to build on this work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- It is not clear how the method proposed in this paper is novel compared to prior work[1]. The paragraph on prior work that compares to black box methods should describe the difference to prior methods better at the end of the paragraph. As well, The method should compare to the algorithm developed in [1].
- The dynamic reward preference rating is similar to prior methods for training successor state representations[2]. it's not clear if the method proposed in the paper for this type of dynamic reweighting is novel.
- More detail should be included on how the microarchitecture is encoded into the neural network for training.
- Why do the authors choose to use the A2C RL algorithm to optimize for the particular architecture and objective in this problem? There are many other options.
- What are golden values? Is that some type of ground truth information?
- Section 4.3 requires more detail. This is a unique application of reinforcement learning to a design problem with more realistic and well-designed simulators, action space and reward functions. These design choices should be described in additional detail to help the readers of the paper understand how the different mechanisms interact, why a particular part of the simulator is chosen and how the training is performed over these particular simulation environments. These details will also help people build on methods like these.
- As a final step for validating the overall design and search space for this type of research, it seems like it would be very beneficial to enact or create the overall designed architecture to prove that the combined algorithm and simulation result in a proper performance architecture.


References:
- [1] Kumar, Aviral, Amir Yazdanbakhsh, Milad Hashemi, Kevin Swersky, and Sergey Levine. 2021. “Data-Driven Offline Optimization For Architecting Hardware Accelerators.” arXiv [cs.AR]. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/ARXIV.2110.11346.
- [2] Barreto, André, Rémi Munos, Tom Schaul, and David Silver. 2016. “Successor Features for Transfer in Reinforcement Learning,” 1–13.
content.summary_of_the_review: Using RL for microarchitecture design seems promising. However, the paper lacks many technical details and comparisons to prior work. I will likely increase the score significantly if these issues are addressed.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper describes a technique to automatically suggest a better design of microcontroller chips using RL. The authors have used RL as an optimization tool and have used simplifications to avert the cost incurred by EDA tools for processor verification. The authors have replaced the EDA tools with lightweight PPA models and software simulation tools to make the RL process produce results faster. 

There is much talk about the reward function but there is as little as one sentence about the action space: "The action space A consists of determinations of hardware resources". If the action selection is independent of each other, meaning all actions can be chosen at random then again it is an optimization problem, not an RL problem. 

There are a few other contributions that authors have made, but there is not much detail given for those. They have calibrated the GEM5 and  McPAT tools using supervised learning. How? that remains undisclosed. 

They have also replaced the EDA tools with lightweight models and simulation tools, but again how effective was this, remained a question. The questions about the deviation from the EDA tools and strategy to mitigate them, and their effects on the learning (optimization) process, all remain unanswered.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The article has presented the detailed result of optimizations achieved by their strategy. They have provided detailed plots of the error rates produced during different experiments. The diagrams are clear and compact, they can be seen in detail after zooming in on the PDF. A reader using printouts might find it difficult to get the information.

Authors have used intuitions without any proof or a scientific basis. For example, in section 3.5 authors say, "We hold the intuition that by calibrating the simulation and modeling tools against golden values generated by EDA tools, we can leverage the calibrated models to predict PPA values for unseen microarchitectures with acceptable accuracy."
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The article is not well structured. At multiple places reader is left with questions unanswered.

The problem has been attempted before, this time an RL technique was used to solve the problem. The problem itself is a multi-objective optimization problem but is posed as an RL problem, although it is possible to solve optimization problems using RL techniques, but that should be stated clearly. In that case, a comparison with the optimization algorithms is more suitable. 

Authors have replaced EDA tools with their own framework, but is this established that the developed lightweight environment is an adequate compensator for the already in-use EDA tools? What differences are there? how much error does it produce in the learning process, and how it is mitigated?
content.summary_of_the_review:
Because the authors are unable to give satisfactory answers to many of the questions raised during the review, and they are unable to provide any information that why they chose an RL algorithm for the optimization problem, I will recommend rejecting the article. 

I am open to admitting that processor architecture is not my domain, but like me, there would be thousands of others who would not know the domain very well but would want to benefit from the article. Here comes the problem of not enlisting the problem adequately. If there is an action space for the problem that restricts the choice of one action based on the previous choice, then this is an RL problem, but that is not clear in the article. The fundamental parts of RL are given almost no importance and the main focus remained on the reward function just like an optimization problem would focus on the objective function formulation and detail.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a reinforcement learning algorithm for optimizing the performance-power-area characteristics of RISC-V Microarchitectures.  They include extensive benchmarking of their approach against other methods, as well as human experts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: The authors do a great job detailing how effectively they can optimize PPA characteristics for a variety of architectures, culminating in Figure 7, which fairly convincingly demonstrates that their method is reliably outperforming humans on the design task (though I might suggest recreating the figure with all scores normalized against human performance---it's a little bit hard to read with all the skinny bars with almost the same lengths).

Weaknesses: It's not clear if the authors plan on releasing their method in any form.  There's also some quality issues throughout discussed more below.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and quality: While the experimental results / general thrust of the paper is clear and of high quality, the presentation has lingering grammatical awkwardness throughout.  The manuscript could use an overhaul to clarify language, and correct spelling mistakes.

Novelty: machine-optimized circuit design is an active space, and this seems like a nontrivial addition to the literature inasmuch as it's convincingly beating human experts.

Reproducibility:  The authors do not provide a reference implementation.  Additionally, it seems like it would be difficult to reproduce the author's work with just a copy of this manuscript (i.e., the entire optimization run by the authors has quite a few moving parts).  This work would be greatly improved by an open sourcing of the method.
content.summary_of_the_review: A compelling advance in the field of automated circuit design, but with some quality issues, and currently not reproducible.
